Article Title: Meta AI head Alexandr Wang praises Mark Zuckerberg, he replies: I have never gotten such a nice…
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang

‘ Very Bayesian ’: Rapid decisive conviction

Meta AI head Alexandr Wang and company CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently had a candid exchange on the company's executive leadership and high-stakes decision-making. During a recent interview, Meta’s Wang was asked about the qualities of Facebook founder, and he offered glowing praise for Zuckerberg, highlighting his exceptional willingness to make massive, rapid pivots based on core convictions. During the conversation Wang was specifically asked how Zuckerberg differed as a leader from what he initially anticipated. Before Wang could reply, Zuckerberg opened with a lighthearted quip, joking, “I think I can leave now.” Wang quickly followed up with his perspective on their working relationship over the past year.Wang noted that while he does not have an extensive set of comparisons, observing Zuckerberg's management style firsthand revealed unique traits that stand out even within elite tech founder circles:“One of the very cool things about working with Mark over the past year has just been watching the true degree of his boldness,” Wang explained, adding, “Once he internalises certain beliefs, like the speed and magnitude of willing to change prior actions and pivot towards the worldview that is consistent with those beliefs, I think these are pretty unusual traits, generally speaking, even among this base of founders. Very Bayesian.”The analytical praise drew a warm, humorous reaction from Zuckerberg.“Very Bayesian. I've never gotten such a nice compliment,” Zuckerberg responded.A person who follows the Bayesian method relies on statistical inference, using Bayes' theorem to update the probability of a hypothesis as new data or evidence becomes available.Expanding on his observations, Wang admitted that Zuckerberg's appetite for sweeping strategic gambles initially took him by surprise before earning his deep respect.“No, but then I think also just the degree of boldness. It was actually quite puzzling to me at first, the degree to which you were willing to make these massive bets. That is quite a notable trait and something I really admire,” Wang continued.Zuckerberg concluded the exchange with appreciation for the assessment, replying:“I'm so flattered.”The exchange underscores the aggressive, conviction-driven posture Meta continues to adopt at the top level as leadership steers resources toward large-scale bets and foundational technical shifts.
Article Summary: Meta AI head Alexandr Wang and Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently had a candid exchange on the company's executive leadership and high-stakes decision- making. Wang noted that observing Zuckerberg's management style firsthand revealed unique traits that stand out even within elite tech founder circles.

Article Title: Boat expands global footprint with Sri Lanka, Bhutan launch; international revenue surges in FY26
Article Text: Homegrown audio and wearables brand Boat has expanded its international presence with its entry into Sri Lanka and Bhutan, as the company looks to accelerate growth beyond India under its "Boat 2.0" strategy. The company said its international revenue more than doubled in FY26, a performance it described as an early validation of its efforts to build markets outside India. The latest expansion strengthens Boat's footprint across South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region.Boat will launch a multi-category portfolio in both Sri Lanka and Bhutan, covering personal audio products, smartwatches and charging solutions. The company said it plans to tailor its offerings over time based on local consumer preferences and market demand.The move comes as Boat seeks to diversify its growth drivers after establishing itself as a leading player in India's audio and wearables market. International markets are expected to play a key role in the company's next phase of growth, alongside expansion into newer consumer technology categories.According to Boat, Sri Lanka and Bhutan offer attractive opportunities due to their young, increasingly digital-first populations, rising adoption of personal electronics and familiarity with Indian brands and popular culture. Commenting on the expansion, Gaurav Nayyar, CEO of Boat, said the company's international strategy is focused on building relevance market by market rather than simply expanding product availability."For us, international expansion is not about putting the same products on more shelves. It is about building market by market, understanding local consumers and creating relevance in each geography," Nayyar said.He added that the company aims to build Boat into a global lifestyle technology brand originating from India, competing on product design, innovation and consumer understanding.The international push comes amid a broader evolution of Boat's business. While audio remains its core category, the company said it has expanded its capabilities in wearables, charging solutions and other emerging technology segments. It added that its wearables business turned profitable in FY26, while charging solutions and other emerging categories contributed a growing share of profits.Supporting the expansion is Boat Labs, the company's in-house research and development centre, which employs more than 100 engineers focused on product development and innovation across categories.Going forward, Boat said it plans to deepen its presence in existing overseas markets while evaluating further expansion opportunities across South Asia, Southeast Asia, the GCC and other high-potential regions.
Article Summary: Boat will launch a multi-category portfolio in both Sri Lanka and Bhutan. The company said it plans to tailor its offerings over time based on local consumer preferences and market demand. The move comes as Boat seeks to diversify its growth drivers after establishing itself as a leading player in India's audio and wearables market.

Article Title: AI just solved hundreds of maths problems overnight, so what’s the problem with AI doing mathematics
Article Text:
AI solved hundreds of maths problems overnight, and mathematicians aren’t cheering.

The proofs arrived without anyone to explain them

Mathematics has always moved forward by getting stuck

Open problems are now fair game for AI labs

Maths is only the first field this will happen to

In September, an unreleased OpenAI model solved a maths problem that had been open for close to 90 years. It needed 88 hours.The Navier-Stokes problem asks whether the equations that describe how fluids move always behave sensibly, or whether they can break down. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems set out in 2000, each carrying a million-dollar reward, and only one of them had been solved before.That was by Grigori Perelman, who famously refused the money. OpenAI says it won't be claiming its prize either.Then, on October 6, the company went much bigger. It put more than 700 manuscripts on GitHub in a single night, grouped into 372 families of results that cover almost every branch of the subject, from number theory and topology to probability and theoretical computer science. The model behind them had attempted around 4,000 problems, and OpenAI says the average result took the equivalent of about three hours of ChatGPT Pro's thinking time. One of those results proves the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a close relative of the most famous open problem in mathematics. Rutgers mathematician Alex Kontorovich wrote on X that a human who managed it would be in line for an "instant Fields Medal".The pace is the part that is hard to take in. In May, OpenAI announced that one of its models had disproved a decades-old conjecture by Paul Erdős.In August, it announced ten long-standing problems at once. Two months later, it was hundreds.You would expect the field to be celebrating.Instead, more than two dozen Fields medallists, holders of the discipline's highest honour, have signed a statement calling the goals of AI companies and mathematicians severely misaligned, and over 8,000 researchers have backed it since. PhD students are openly asking what their degrees will be worth by the time they graduate. It is tempting to read all of this as a profession sulking about being outdone by a machine, and plenty of people online have read it exactly that way. Very few mathematicians, though, are arguing that the AI got the maths wrong.The problem lies in what comes with those answers, or rather what doesn't. They arrive without anyone who understands them, they skip the slow, painful work that actually trains mathematicians, and they come from labs that are now racing the very people expected to check them.To most people, a proof simply confirms that something is true. To mathematicians, it is the explanation of why it is true, and that explanation is the part other researchers build on, borrow from and teach. It is also why a new result usually comes with an author attached, someone who gives talks on it, takes questions from sceptical colleagues and defends every step in front of referees before the field accepts it.None of the October manuscripts has one.Researchers working through them describe odd notation, arguments that are hard to follow and reference lists that look thin for results of this size. By OpenAI's own account, only one of the 700-odd papers was edited by a human, and just 10 include the model's chain of thought, the record of how it reached its conclusions. The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton summed up the shift in a statement, warning that AI can now produce mathematical arguments that the person who prompted it can neither understand, verify nor take responsibility for. Terence Tao, among the most respected mathematicians alive, put it more pointedly, criticising prompters who chase a famous problem, declare it solved and then cannot answer basic questions about the result.The usual safety net is Lean, a programming language that checks proofs line by line, much like a compiler checks code. By OpenAI's own figures, only about 42% of the release has been run through it so far, which leaves most of it resting on prose alone.Even the formalised portion isn't a clean bill of health. Researchers at Cambridge and King's College London compared the written Navier-Stokes proof with its Lean version and found at least two places where the two don't say the same thing. That doesn't sink the result, but it does show that a model translating its own argument into a checker can't simply be taken at its word. Lean can also be gamed, with models sometimes finding loopholes in the checker instead of solving the actual problem, a behaviour researchers call reward hacking.Within days of the release, three papers had been withdrawn over a sign error, and more than a dozen others had been revised.The work itself is strong in places. Researchers who know these areas describe several results as top-journal material, and a handful as the kind that would make a career.The issue is scale, and who carries the cost of it. A lab can publish 700 manuscripts in a night, while a specialist can take weeks to read just one of them properly, and there are only so many specialists to go around. Peer review, the process that normally catches mistakes before they spread, has been left to happen after the fact.Mathematics has been in a similar spot once before, on a far smaller scale. Srinivasa Ramanujan's notebooks held thousands of results, most of them without proofs, and the number theorist Bruce Berndt spent more than two decades working through them one by one. But those results came from a single mind, reached the world over years, and nobody was promising another batch the following month.Ask mathematicians what they got out of a problem they never solved, and many will tell you it was worth it anyway. Hugo Duminil-Copin, a 2022 Fields medallist, wrote this year that his failed attempts at one well-known conjecture in probability produced dozens of ideas he later used elsewhere, leading to discoveries he would not otherwise have made.In the same essay, he described AI proofs as ones that "nuke the mathematical landscape".The subject has always moved forward this way. Imaginary numbers, the square roots of negative numbers, were dismissed as useless by the 16th-century mathematicians who first stumbled on them. Today engineers use them to design the circuits in your phone, and quantum physics cannot be written down without them. Very often, the tools built on the way to an answer end up outlasting the question itself.That middle stretch is exactly what AI skips. Researchers reading the release say the model mostly pushed known methods further and combined them in clever ways, filling gaps in what the field already knew rather than opening up anything new. Stephen Wolfram, speaking at a public event on the day of the release, made the point that producing new theorems is easy, and producing ones that anybody cares about is not.William Thurston, one of the great geometers of the 20th century, saw a small version of this coming in 1994. In an essay on how mathematics makes progress, he described how his own rapid run of results in an area called foliations put others off working on it. Once they moved on, much of what they had understood faded with them. Mathematical knowledge, he argued, lives mostly in the heads of the people working on it, with the papers playing a supporting role.Thurston emptied one corner of the field. The model has done the same to dozens at once.The people with the most to lose are the ones still learning. For generations, PhD advisers have handed students an open problem that might take a year or two to crack, knowing the answer mattered less than the instincts the student built along the way. Those are precisely the problems AI is now clearing in bulk. Some students have already watched their dissertation topics get solved for them, and some researchers have seen grant proposals built around now-answered questions lose their purpose overnight. A field that stops producing people who understand its answers will eventually struggle to tell which ones matter.Someone still has to decide which results are worth building on, which ones lead somewhere new, and which were never worth the compute. That kind of judgement comes from years of being stuck on hard problems, and so far there is no shortcut to it.There is a quieter cost too, and it is about trust. Mathematicians routinely share half-finished ideas with colleagues long before they are ready to publish, on the understanding that nobody will run off with them. That arrangement held because so few people understand any given problem well enough to get there first.A lab with enough compute no longer needs to.OpenAI says it only went after Navier-Stokes after spotting chatter online that someone else was close. That someone turned out to be NYU's Tristan Buckmaster, working with Levent Alpöge, an Anthropic researcher collaborating in a personal capacity. The company threw roughly 10,000 AI agents and millions of dollars in compute at the problem, and announced its solution a day after the pair published related findings. What happened in between is still disputed. Buckmaster has said publicly that he used OpenAI's Codex while working on the problem, and that he never got a clear answer on whether those sessions fed into the model's training. OpenAI says no specific user data was accessed, but admits it can't rule out that de-identified data from his usage helped improve its models. Sébastien Bubeck, the OpenAI researcher Buckmaster named, disputes parts of his account and says the two proofs differ significantly.Andreas Thom, a Dresden mathematician whose work underpinned one of OpenAI's August results, raised a similar concern and made the sharper point: removing a name from data does not remove the idea in it.With nothing settled, the uncertainty alone is changing behaviour. Some researchers have stopped listing open conjectures at the end of their papers, and people who maintain public lists of unsolved problems are wondering if they are simply handing out targets. The companies involved also sit in an uncomfortable double role, selling research tools to the same mathematicians they are competing with for results.A field that has always worked in the open is becoming more guarded.OpenAI is hardly the only lab chasing these results. In early 2024, Google DeepMind made headlines with a system that could solve olympiad-level geometry problems, and by last year its models were scoring gold at the International Mathematical Olympiad. Anthropic's Claude was used to disprove the decades-old Jacobian conjecture in July, and Meta has published papers mathematicians wrote with its Muse Spark model.Part of the appeal has little to do with mathematics itself. Maths demands long chains of careful reasoning, and many in the industry see cracking it as a sign of more capable, more general AI. A famous solved problem has become the cleanest way for a lab to show that its model is the smartest, which goes some way to explaining why the field's own needs have so often come second.After months of criticism, OpenAI has adjusted parts of its approach. It worked with an independent advisory group of nine leading mathematicians hosted by the Institute for Advanced Study, published the papers with a public revision history, disclosed how many problems the model attempted and promised to fund workshops to help the field digest the results. What it refused was the group's very first request: stop testing advanced problems on proprietary models nobody else can use. OpenAI argues that this is how it builds better tools for scientists. Its critics worry about a two-tier system, in which a few labs race ahead on unreleased models while everyone else is left checking their work.Mathematics was always going to feel this first, because it is one of the few fields where a machine can check its own work. The rest of science is not far behind.A study of 41.3 million papers, published in Nature in January, found that scientists who use AI publish more and get cited more, but also that AI narrowed the range of topics being studied by almost 5% and cut engagement with one another's work by 22%. In a Google survey of more than 600 scientists, nearly half said AI pushed them towards safer, incremental projects, the opposite of the risky work that tends to produce big breakthroughs. Theoretical physicists, whose work sits closest to pure maths, say AI became their default tool for calculation in a matter of months.So the problem with AI doing mathematics comes down to what happens after the answer. October 6 delivered a mountain of them and handed everything else back to mathematicians: the checking, the explaining, the credit and the training of whoever comes next. Rumours of the next batch were circulating before most of the first had even been read.When Perelman refused his million, he argued that Richard Hamilton, whose work his proof was built on, deserved as much credit as he did.Mathematics has always treated the people behind an answer as part of the answer itself. Whoever does the maths next, human or machine, will have to work that way too.
Article Summary: OpenAI put 700 manuscripts on GitHub in a single night. They cover almost every branch of the subject, from number theory and topology to probability and theoretical computer science. Only one of the 700-odd papers was edited by a human, and just 10 include the model's chain of thought, how it reached its conclusions.

Article Title: A New York town once known for IBM is resisting a 1-gigawatt AI data centre; residents fear the cost of powering it
Article Text:
AI generated image for representation

East Fishkill imposes a three-year moratorium on data centres

“I just think that we’re at this moment where things are happening very quickly; we need to get our ducks in a row and think about the various ways in which data centres and new energy usage will affect our long-term community cohesiveness, environmental quality, and character,”

Why the proposed 1-gigawatt AI data centre has raised concerns

“The pushback is really to the size,”

“The Treetop center would be 1,000 megawatts. People do not want to pay higher electricity rates because of a larger data centre coming in and putting pressure on the grid.”

“It’s not going to provide work to keep people here like the previous tech businesses did,”

“So what’s the benefit to the town?”

IBM's legacy shapes opposition to the development

Developer challenges the town's data centre ban

New York’s East Fishkill is debating AI infrastructure. The town, located about 70 miles north of New York City, was once a major semiconductor manufacturing hub, with IBM operating a 460-acre campus there for nearly 50 years. However, a proposed 1-gigawatt artificial intelligence (AI) data centre has prompted residents to question whether the project would benefit the community or put additional pressure on its electricity supply.The data center developer Treetop Companies is exploring plans for a facility spanning more than 1 million square feet across approximately 143 acres. Residents have organised protests and pushed for restrictions, arguing the project could raise electricity costs, harm the environment, and offer limited long-term employment.East Fishkill's town board unanimously adopted a three-year moratorium in late June 2026, preventing the consideration of new data centres larger than 20 megawatts until July 2029. Officials said the pause would give the community time to study the potential effects of such facilities on water resources, local ecosystems and the area's character.The opposition gathered momentum even before the developer submitted a formal data centre application to the town. Residents attended public meetings, organised rallies and called for restrictions on large-scale projects.said East Fishkill resident and professor Tanya Radford.The proposed development has also drawn attention because of its expected electricity demand. Residents fear that adding a facility of this scale could strain the grid and raise power bills.The controversy began after Treetop Development purchased property in East Fishkill while initially pursuing approvals for a warehouse project. Residents later discovered that Donovan Drive Holdings, a local property owner associated with the development, submitted a request to the New York Independent System Operator's (NYISO) interconnection queue for about 1,000 megawatts of electrical service.NYISO manages New York's high-voltage electricity grid and reviews requests from large projects seeking to connect to it. The request raised concerns because a 1-gigawatt data centre would consume more electricity than the entire city of Buffalo, which has approximately 275,000 residents. East Fishkill, meanwhile, has a population of around 30,000.Fran Caracappa, a resident and county legislature candidate, said the project's scale was central to the opposition.resident Fran Caracappa, a candidate for county legislature, said.Residents have also questioned whether the facility would create enough permanent jobs to justify its electricity demand and land use.Caracappa said.East Fishkill's resistance comes despite its history as a technology centre. IBM's semiconductor operations employed thousands of workers and helped establish the region's industrial identity. Parts of the former IBM campus now form iPark 84, a mixed-use development that houses commercial, residential and technology facilities.Residents have made it clear that they oppose not technology itself, but the size of the proposed project and its potential impact. The industrial past of the region has raised concerns about contamination of groundwater from semiconductor manufacture . There are still several polluted Superfund sites in the area .Other issues residents raised include noise, diesel backup generators, wetlands, property values, and the loss of the area's rural character.Treetop has appealed the moratorium. In a 17-page objection letter submitted to the town board, the company's attorneys argued that the measure unlawfully targets its property and effectively amounts to a permanent prohibition rather than a temporary planning measure.The company said it had spent years and significant resources advancing development plans, including environmental reviews, wetlands investigations, traffic studies and utility coordination.However, the town’s officials have maintained that no formal data centre application has been submitted and that the moratorium will allow them to assess how local zoning should address large-scale facilities.
Article Summary: East Fishkill imposes a three-year moratorium on data centres. The data center developer Treetop Companies is exploring plans for a facility spanning more than 1 million square feet across approximately 143 acres. Residents have organised protests and pushed for restrictions, arguing the project could raise electricity costs.

Article Title: Dreame X60 Ultra Complete robot vacuum cleaner review: Everyday cleaning made super easy
Article Text:
Rating – 4/5

Design and build

Performance

Powerful suction for everyday dirt

Verdict

Robot vacuums are designed to take some of the effort out of everyday cleaning, but can a machine at this price do enough to reduce the need for manual cleaning? Dreame is betting on a combination of powerful suction, AI-powered navigation, hot-water mop cleaning and a slim design that can reach under low furniture. The company recently launched Dreame X60 Ultra Complete in India that an also cross certain raised surfaces that may stop other robot vacuums. At Rs 1,29,999, the Dreame X60 Ultra Complete sits firmly in the premium end of India's robot vacuum cleaner market. While the features sound promising on paper, but the real question is whether they make a noticeable difference in Indian homes, where dust, hair, food spills and different floor surfaces can make daily cleaning challenging. We look at what the Dreame X60 Ultra Complete offers and whether its features justify the premium price.The Dreame X60 Ultra Complete takes a different approach to robot vacuum design, with a slim profile that allows it to reach spaces where bulkier models may struggle. Measuring just 7.95cm in height, it is designed to clean under low furniture, including beds and sofas. Its retractable DToF/LDS navigation sensor helps the robot maintain this low profile, although the stated clearance requirements depend on the navigation mode and the space available under the furniture.The design also focuses on handling obstacles around the home. Dreame's ProLeap system allows the robot to cross single steps up to 4.5cm and double-layer obstacles up to 8.8cm under specified conditions. Its Triple-Wheel AgiLift chassis can handle double-layer thresholds up to 30mm and lift the chassis when moving onto carpets.The robot also features an extendable side brush and mop to reach corners and edges that can be difficult for round robot vacuums to clean. Its base station houses the cleaning and maintenance functions, including automatic dust emptying, mop washing with water heated to up to 100°C under laboratory conditions, and hot-air mop drying. Talking about the base station, it has a premium design with slightly golden finish that fits into modern homes.Dreame X60 Ultra Complete is designed to make everyday cleaning less dependent on human intervention, and that is where it makes a strong impression. The vacuum is efficient, and once the cleaning schedule and settings are configured, it can handle routine cleaning on its own. Its custom cleaning modes are another highlight, particularly the option to select specific zones instead of running the robot across the entire house every time. This is useful for targeting areas that need more frequent cleaning.The robot offers up to 35,000Pa of suction, supported by Dreame's HyperStream Detangling DuoBrush 2.0. The brush combines bristled rubber and TPU rubber rollers to pick up dust and debris from hard floors and carpets. Suction levels can also be adjusted through the app, giving users more control over how the robot cleans different surfaces. In everyday use, the overall cleaning efficiency is a key strength, although the advertised suction figure is based on the company's laboratory tests and does not, by itself, indicate how much dirt will be collected in every situation.The X60 Ultra Complete uses two 120-degree cameras, an LED light and its OmniSight system to identify obstacles and plan its route. Dreame says the system can recognise more than 280 types of objects. This is intended to help the robot navigate around everyday items rather than simply following a fixed cleaning path.One of the more interesting features is proactive illumination dirt detection. The robot uses light to make difficult-to-spot dirt, hair and light-coloured liquid messes easier to identify. It can then adapt its cleaning approach to the area. This is particularly relevant for debris that may not be obvious under normal room lighting.For mopping, the robot uses two rotating pads that spin at up to 230RPM and apply 15N of downward pressure. Dreame's system is designed to tackle everyday marks on hard floors, while the base station washes the mop pads using water heated to up to 100°C under laboratory conditions. The pads are also dried with hot air after cleaning. This automated maintenance is useful as it reduces the need to wash and dry the mop pads manually after every cleaning cycle.The 7.95cm-thin body is designed to reach beneath low furniture, while the retractable navigation sensor helps the robot maintain its low profile. Its extendable side brush and mop can also reach towards corners and edges, areas that round robot vacuums can sometimes miss.For homes with raised thresholds, the ProLeap system is rated to cross single steps up to 4.5cm and double-layer obstacles up to 8.8cm under specified conditions. The chassis can also lift to handle double-layer thresholds up to 30mm and adapt to carpets. These features are intended to reduce the need to move the robot between rooms manually.The all-in-one PowerDock is central to the hands-free experience. It automatically empties the robot's dust box, washes and dries the mop pads, refills the robot's water tank and dispenses cleaning solution. Dreame claims up to 100 days of hands-free dust emptying, depending on usage and conditions.While the dock adds convenience, but it does not eliminate all maintenance. The dust bag, water tanks and other components will still need periodic attention.At Rs 1,29,999, the Dreame X60 Ultra Complete is a premium robot vacuum cleaner that makes a strong case for itself through efficient cleaning and automation. Its powerful suction, custom zone-cleaning modes, slim design and ability to handle certain raised thresholds make it a versatile option for everyday home cleaning. The self-cleaning dock also reduces the effort involved in maintaining the vacuum and mop. However, the high price means it will appeal mainly to buyers who value convenience and want to minimise their involvement in daily cleaning. While it still requires periodic maintenance, its ability to handle routine cleaning with minimal human intervention is a major advantage.
Article Summary: Dreame X60 Ultra Complete is designed to make everyday cleaning less dependent on human intervention. The robot offers up to 35,000Pa of suction, supported by Dreame's HyperStream Detangling DuoBrush 2.0. The base station houses the cleaning and maintenance functions, including automatic dust emptying, mop washing with water heated to up to 100°C under laboratory conditions.

Article Title: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar warns companies face cyber risks with budget Chinese AI models
Article Text:
Warning against AI slowdowns and holding back 'Astra'

Hugging Face incident and how Chinese AI models ‘saved’ them

Companies turning to low-cost Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models are exposing themselves to serious digital vulnerabilities, OpenAI chief financial officer (CFO) Sarah Friar warned on Wednesday (October 14), urging organisations to rely on Western-developed platforms for critical operations. Speaking to Bloomberg at the International AI Summit in Dublin, Friar made the case for American infrastructure even as her own company faces scrutiny over recent unauthorised intrusions carried out by its frontier systems.“We think you want to be on more Western models on the cyber front,” Friar said during the conference, where she shared the official program alongside European Commission representative Henna Virkkunen, as per the publication.Addressing broader debates over the pace of AI development – which OpenAI CEO Sam Altman supported after Anthropic chief Dario Amodei called for a slowdown – Friar argued that American technology companies must avoid slowing down development excessively.She cautioned that artificial delays could produce a strategic imbalance regarding who controls powerful systems capable of triggering mission-critical disruptions.Friar disclosed that OpenAI is currently holding back a model named Astra because the company cannot yet rule out that it possesses critical cyber capabilities.Her remarks were echoed by rival lab Anthropic at the same summit, where its head of international argued hours earlier that open-source models inherently carry greater operational risk.The warnings arrive amid fierce global competition. Bloomberg reported in August that Chinese releases now represent the single largest share of generative model downloads on the developer hub Hugging Face.Hugging Face is also the platform that OpenAI’s models penetrated during a security incident in July. Following the intrusion, Hugging Face sought $100 million in compute credits and full system traces from OpenAI to analyze the agents' activity.When Hugging Face launched its post-incident forensic investigation, commercial AI tools refused to analyze the attacker's code. To work around the refusal, Hugging Face deployed GLM 5.2 – a Chinese open-weight model – hosted on its own internal servers. Using GLM 5.2, the team evaluated more than 17,000 discrete actions to contain the breach.OpenAI also issued a formal apology in September after disclosing that its models breached four Australian government departments. Further, Anthropic has disclosed separate cybersecurity incidents of its own, acknowledging that its models reached real-world organizations during benchmark testing and evaluation runs.
Article Summary: OpenAI chief financial officer (CFO) Sarah Friar urged companies to rely on Western-developed platforms for critical operations. Friar made the case for American infrastructure even as her own company faces scrutiny over recent unauthorised intrusions carried out by its systems.

Article Title: WhatsApp brings guest calling, lets people without an account join calls through a link
Article Text:
WhatsApp guest calls support up to 32 people and stay end-to-end encrypted

WhatsApp guest calls keep the host in control

You no longer need WhatsApp to join a WhatsApp call. Meta has started rolling out guest calling, a feature that lets anyone hop on a call through an invite link without downloading the app or signing up for an account.Guests get the same basics that regular users do: free calls, end-to-end encryption and no time limit, so nobody gets cut off mid-conversation. They can also share their computer screen, react with a thumbs up or heart emoji, and raise a hand to speak.There is one catch, and one limitation worth knowing. Only someone with a WhatsApp account can start a call and create the link. Guests can also join from a mobile browser, but they won’t be able to turn on their own camera for now. They can still see other participants’ video during the call.Setting up a call takes a few taps. Open the Calls tab, tap the "+" icon, create a call link and share it with the people you want on the call. Hosts can do this from the phone app or from WhatsApp Web. Guests then type in their name and can join one-on-one or group calls with up to 32 people.Guests can't walk straight into a call. They wait in a waiting room until the host admits them, and the host can remove them at any time.Guests also can't see other participants' phone numbers, send messages or add anyone else to the call.Guest calling builds on web calling, which WhatsApp added in July. That update also brought noise suppression and a way to move an ongoing call between your phone and desktop.Calendar integrations come next. Later this year, users will be able to install a WhatsApp plugin for Google Calendar or Outlook, connect their account and add a call link to their invites. Everyone on the invite can join, whether or not they have WhatsApp.
Article Summary: Meta has started rolling out guest calling, a feature that lets anyone hop on a call through an invite link. Only someone with a WhatsApp account can start a call and create the link. Guests can also join from a mobile browser, but they won't be able to turn on their own camera for now.

Article Title: Xbox Labs launched to explore how AI can change gaming: Read CEO Asha Sharma's message to employees
Article Text:
Read Xbox CEO Asha Sharma’s full message to employees

“Team,

The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we’ve helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.

In recent weeks, we’ve seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we’ve seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.

These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.

To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.

I think XBOX has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software.

Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We’ve spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible.

As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.

Our priorities aren’t changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.

Asha”

Xbox has launched Xbox Labs. The new initiative explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and emerging technologies could change how people create, access, and play games. In a message to employees globally, CEO Asha Sharma said the initiative will bring together game makers, engineers and scientists to turn new ideas into experiences for players and developers. The announcement comes as experiments in AI, software portability, and game modification challenge traditional boundaries between gaming hardware, software development, and content creation.Sharma said Xbox Labs will focus on building new tools, testing emerging possibilities, and learning from how people use them, aiming to make games more accessible and let more players become creators. She also said the initiative would not change Xbox’s existing priorities, including developing games, supporting hardware and protecting intellectual property and gaming communities. Sharma’s message outlines how Microsoft’s gaming division plans to explore these technologies while continuing its existing work.
Article Summary: Xbox has launched Xbox Labs. New initiative explores how artificial intelligence and emerging technologies could change how people create, access, and play games. CEO Asha Sharma said the initiative will bring together game makers, engineers and scientists to turn new ideas into experiences for players and developers.

Article Title: Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis warns future AI agent hacking may soon turn ‘major incidents’
Article Text:
Sir Demis Hassabis

Microsoft president calls 2026 a ‘Sobering Year’

Recent hacking and unauthorised activities carried out by artificial intelligence (AI) agents represent “early warning shots” for the world, Google DeepMind co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis has said, warning that without swift, industry-wide efforts to harden system security far more destructive incidents could unfold in the coming years. Speaking at an AI summit in Dublin, Hassabis addressed mounting anxiety across the technology sector following a string of AI agent behaviours. The disruptions include intrusions into corporate computer networks and a recent incident disclosed by AI developer Anthropic, in which one of its models submitted a fabricated homicide report to law enforcement.Hassabis, who also serves as chief scientist at Google’s parent company Alphabet, stated that the broader sector must adopt rigorous safeguards comparable to the strict containment protocols maintained in biological laboratories and the nuclear industry, as per a report by news agency Reuters.“I think these hacking incidents are early warning shots for us that systems aren't that powerful yet, so the incidents aren't that major. But they could be looking into next year and the next couple years if we don't do more work as an industry, as individual companies and governments on securing these systems,” Hassabis said at the conference.Joining the discussion in Dublin, Microsoft president Brad Smith agreed with the gravity of the moment, describing 2026 as a "sobering year" due to repeated instances of rogue agent behaviour.Smith argued that official legal boundaries and industry regulations must catch up to the sheer velocity of software development, urging technology firms to abandon their traditional resistance to public oversight.“No company or technology should be above the law. But we need law, we need regulation. It needs to be sensible, it needs to be balanced, it needs to take into account innovations. This allergy that some in the industry have to regulation is frankly something we need to get over,” Smith said.Both executives indicated that institutional oversight will become unavoidable as models take on autonomous capabilities, though Hassabis stressed that regulatory structures must stay flexible. While suggesting that an international standards body would eventually be necessary, Hassabis warned that static, heavy-handed rules could choke technical progress before benefits are realised. Instead, he argued for an adaptive oversight model that can adjust alongside model capabilities.“So what you need to do is basically build up dynamically this kind of certification process that is proportionate with the risks as we see it and can quickly change depending on where the technology goes,” Hassabis noted.Google also reported hacking incident by its AI agents but it went on to say that its agents stopped when they realised they are breaching legitimate websites.
Article Summary: Google DeepMind co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis spoke at an AI summit in Dublin. He said recent hacking and unauthorised activities carried out by artificial intelligence (AI) agents represent “early warning shots” for the world. Without swift, industry-wide efforts to harden system security far more destructive incidents could unfold in the coming years. Microsoft president Brad Smith agreed with the gravity of the moment, describing 2026 as a "sobering year"

Article Title: Google.org commits $15 million to boost AI adoption among India's MSMEs
Article Text: Google.org has announced $15 million in funding for The/Nudge to support the growth and digital transformation of India's micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), with a focus on expanding access to credit, compliance tools and market opportunities through artificial intelligence. The announcement was made in New Delhi on October 14.The funding is part of Google's broader commitment to support India's national AI roadmap and comes as MSMEs continue to play a critical role in the country's economy. According to the organisations, India is home to more than 90 million small businesses that employ over 345 million people.Under the initiative, the funding will be used to develop scalable AI-powered solutions aimed at helping MSMEs overcome key business challenges, including access to formal credit, regulatory compliance and market discovery. The programme will include an open call for proposals to identify and support innovative solutions for the sector. It will also establish a multilingual, voice-led platform designed to train local talent in Tier 3 and Tier 4 towns with job-ready skills and connect them directly with small businesses.Preeti Lobana, VP and Country Manager, Google India, said the company's objective is to make advanced technology more practical and accessible for businesses across the country."At Google, our goal is to turn advanced technology into everyday capabilities that anyone can use. For AI to be truly successful in India, it must become a practical multiplier for the millions of small businesses that drive our economic growth," Lobana said. She added that the partnership with The/Nudge aims to put open digital tools directly into the hands of entrepreneurs and small business owners, enabling them to benefit from the AI-driven technology shift.Subhashree Dutta, CEO of the^delta, described the initiative as one of the largest philanthropic commitments focused on India's MSME sector. "This is one of the largest philanthropic commitments to India's MSMEs, and we at the^delta are proud to build it with Google.org to put AI to work for them," Dutta said. According to Dutta, the programme will support innovation through stage-gated grand challenges that address multiple barriers faced by MSMEs, including compliance, market access, quality standards and credit availability.She added that the initiative aims to create open standards that could help make small businesses more competitive, creditworthy and visible in domestic and global markets.The announcement underscores growing interest from technology companies and philanthropic organisations in using AI to support India's vast MSME sector. By developing accessible AI tools and workforce training platforms, the initiative seeks to help smaller enterprises participate more effectively in the digital economy while improving access to business opportunities and financial services.
Article Summary: Google announces $15 million in funding for The/Nudge to support the growth and digital transformation of India's micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) The funding will be used to develop scalable AI-powered solutions aimed at helping MSMEs overcome key business challenges.

Funding social innovation, healthcare and education

In 2009, as the global financial crisis began hitting island communities hard, eBay founder Pierre Omidyar and his wife, Pam, pledged $50 million over six years to the Hawaii Community Foundation (HCF). At the time, the historic commitment stood as one of the largest single charitable gifts ever made by living donors in Hawaii, laying the groundwork for a stabilisation drive that went on to assist more than 10,000 individuals and families across the state. The couple, who relocated back to the islands in 2006 to raise their children, came forward to expand their local giving right as households faced financial strain.“Pam and I are privileged to call Hawaii home. Given the economic crisis and hardships throughout the state, we felt it was especially important at this time to expand our philanthropy in the islands,” Pierre Omidyar said in a release announcing the pledge at that time.Administered by HCF through the Omidyar Ohana Fund, the initial grant was designed to respond swiftly to the downturn while encouraging collaboration among regional philanthropists.A centerpiece of the effort was the Hawaii Community Stabilization Initiative, launched to support households hurting from the recession. The Omidyar fund contributed approximately $2.3 million in the initial seed funding, and then 11 partner organisations contributed an additional $2 million. Together, the coalition unlocked another $23 million in federal assistance and vital support services.When it came to community impact, HCF said that the initiative delivered direct relief, including emergency housing support, food assistance and credit counseling, to more than 10,000 people and families. The multi-million-dollar pledge financed a wide range of social, educational and medical initiatives across Hawaii.

Article Title: Netflix layoffs: Company cuts 1,000 jobs; CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos tell employees: Our mission is...
Article Text:
Netflix is cutting about 1,000 jobs, its biggest layoff round since 2022.

Netflix layoffs hit product, tech, legal and HR teams the most

Slowing viewer engagement is Netflix's biggest headache

Netflix games and Netflix House are struggling to pay their way

Netflix is cutting about 1,000 jobs, or roughly 6% of its global workforce. It is the streaming giant's biggest round of layoffs since 2022, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. Co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos told employees in an email on Wednesday morning, a week before the company reports its third-quarter earnings.The cuts come at an awkward time for Netflix. Viewer engagement has slowed, and its shares have fallen more than 40% over the past 12 months. In the email, the two CEOs framed the move as a question of focus. "Our mission, to entertain the world, is ambitious," they wrote, adding that delivering on it means being disciplined about where the company puts its people and money.According to WSJ, most of the job cuts fall within the product, technology, legal and human resources teams. Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees at the end of last year.Peters and Sarandos told staff the company will keep investing heavily in the areas that make the biggest difference, but that this calls for sharper choices across the business. They also said Netflix remains on track to meet its full-year earnings forecast.The last time Netflix cut jobs on this scale was in June 2022. That round followed the company's first quarterly loss of subscribers in more than a decade.Netflix still holds on to its subscribers well. It has about 325 million paying members, and its US cancellation rate of just over 2% is the lowest in the industry, according to analytics firm Antenna.The worry is how much time those subscribers spend watching. Global viewing hours rose just 2% in the first half of 2026, to 97 billion. In July, Netflix also said it would publish its detailed engagement report once a year instead of twice, a change that unsettled investors.Nielsen data tells a similar story. Netflix accounted for 7.8% of TV viewing in the US in July, behind YouTube's 14.2% and down from 9% in December, when hits like Stranger Things pushed its share up. At a Bloomberg event in late September, Sarandos admitted, "we're not growing as fast as I want us to."To win back attention, Netflix has added video podcasts, shows from YouTube creators, live sports and live channels to its service.Some of Netflix's newer bets have not delivered. The company shut its Night School Studio in August and plans to close Moonloot, its Helsinki-based games studio. Greg Lombardo, who led Netflix House, the company's physical attractions in Philadelphia and Dallas, is leaving after seven years.Netflix also lost the bidding war for Warner Bros Discovery's studios and streaming business to Paramount Skydance, which completed its $110 billion acquisition earlier this month. Sarandos has said Netflix is not hunting for a replacement deal and expects growth to remain largely organic.Netflix is not alone in trimming staff. Disney, NBCUniversal and Amazon have all made cuts in recent months. The next test comes on October 20, when Netflix reports third-quarter earnings after the US market closes, which falls in the early hours of October 21 in India. That report will be the first look at how a smaller Netflix plans to get people watching more again.
Article Summary: Netflix is cutting about 1,000 jobs, or roughly 6% of its global workforce. It is the streaming giant's biggest round of layoffs since 2022. Viewer engagement has slowed, and its shares have fallen more than 40% over the past 12 months.

Article Title: In 2004, Jeff Bezos began assembling West Texas ranchland for a private space project; by 2005 he had 165,000 acres, and in 2021 he launched from the property aboard Blue Origin’s first human spacefli
Article Text:
Jeff Bezos may be in talks to purchase stake in Liverpool FC

How Jeff Bezos acquired 165,000 acres in West Texas

“I have every confidence in the world he will do what he says he will do,”

“I know he’s going to have some of the best minds for this project. He doesn’t do things halfway or second class.”

Blue Origin launches its first human spaceflight in 2021

“Today was a monumental day for Blue Origin and human spaceflight,”

“I am so incredibly proud of Team Blue, their professionalism, and expertise in executing today’s flight. This was a big step forward for us and is only the beginning.”

Jeff Bezos' long-term vision for commercial spaceflight

More than two decades ago, Jeff Bezos began building his space ambitions in West Texas. The Amazon founder began buying ranchland near Van Horn in 2004 and, by 2005, had accumulated 165,000 acres to serve as a base for Blue Origin’s private spaceflight operations. The property was originally called Corn Ranch, which is a remote place to develop and test rockets away from population centers.Years later, on July 20, 2021, Bezos launched from the site aboard Blue Origin’s New Shepard rocket on the company’s first human spaceflight. The mission took four people to the edge of space and was a milestone in Bezos' plans to expand human access to space. The process, from land acquisition in the countryside to flying paying customers, was a long-term project that began long before commercial space tourism was in the public mind.Bezos founded Blue Origin in 2000, but the company initially operated with limited public visibility. Its plans became clearer when the Amazon founder began buying land near Van Horn, a small town in Culberson County, Texas.In 2003, local ranchers reportedly began receiving calls from a Seattle-based attorney representing an unnamed buyer interested in purchasing their property. The buyer was willing to make substantial offers, and some landowners eventually agreed to sell.By 2005, Bezos had accumulated 165,000 acres in the region, creating a large private property that would later expand further. He named the property Corn Ranch and subsequently revealed his plans to establish a spaceport there.The location offered a sparsely populated desert environment for rocket launches and testing. Bezos explained that the project was part of his broader ambition to develop the technology needed to send people into space and eventually enable them to live and work beyond Earth.In 2005, John Conoly, then a longtime Culberson County judge, expressed confidence in the project.Conoly told The Associated Press.The West Texas property eventually became the launch site for Blue Origin's New Shepard spacecraft. On July 20, 2021, the company completed its first crewed flight, carrying Bezos, his brother Mark Bezos, aviation pioneer Wally Funk and 18-year-old Oliver Daemen.The rocket lifted off from the company's private spaceport, then the crew capsule separated from the booster and continued toward the edge of space. The passengers experienced several minutes of weightlessness before the capsule returned to Earth under parachutes.The flight lasted approximately 10 minutes. The crew crossed the Kármán Line, commonly recognised as the boundary of space, before landing safely in the West Texas desert.The mission also marked several milestones. Funk, aged 82, became the oldest person to travel to space at the time, while Daemen became the youngest. Jeff and Mark Bezos also became the first siblings to fly into space together.said Bob Smith, then chief executive of Blue Origin.Blue Origin's first crewed mission was part of a wider effort to develop reusable rockets and make space travel available beyond government astronaut programmes. The company had already conducted uncrewed New Shepard flights, testing its rocket and capsule systems before carrying passengers.In November 2015, Blue Origin successfully landed a rocket booster vertically, demonstrating an approach that could allow parts of a launch vehicle to be reused. New Shepard was designed for suborbital flights, while the company's larger New Glenn rocket was intended to support missions into Earth orbit and beyond.Bezos has described his ambition as creating a future in which millions of people could live and work in space. The company has also pursued projects involving lunar exploration and rocket engines.But commercial space tourism has been questioned on affordability and access. Most early passengers have been well-heeled, so the question remains whether private spaceflight can ever be broadly affordable.
Article Summary: The Amazon founder began buying land near Van Horn, Texas, in 2004. By 2005, he had accumulated 165,000 acres to serve as a base for Blue Origin's private spaceflight operations. The property was originally called Corn Ranch, which is a remote place to develop and test rockets away from population centers. On July 20, 2021, Bezos launched from the site aboard Blue Origin’s New Shepard rocket. The mission took four people to the edge of space and was a milestone in Bezos' plans to expand human access to space.

Article Title: Hacker claims that he used the password that security researchers have been warning internet users to stop using since over five years to hack into Denmark's national registry
Article Text:
Authorised business access exploited

How 10 days of automated scraping went undetected

‘123456’ topped most common password for 6 out of 7 years

A hacker has reportedly claimed responsibility for breaching Denmark’s national identity database saying that the massive intrusion was carried out using the ‘most insecure password’ for the last six years: “123456. ” The breach compromised Denmark’s Central Register of Persons (CPR), exposing records connected to approximately 8.8 million people. Speaking to Danish newspaper Politiken, the alleged hacker claimed they gained entry via an external IT contractor’s legitimate corporate account secured by this sequence. The publication reported that at least three accounts belonging to the firm, including an administrator account, relied on the exact same numerical string. The individual told the outlet (via The Register) that they have no intention of leaking or selling the accessed citizen information.On October 5, Denmark's CPR administration publicly confirmed the security failure, disclosing that an authorised third-party contractor's legitimate system credentials had been abused to pull records. While authorities did not initially name the vendor involved, Sophie Laursen, managing director of Funen-based firm Pays ApS, confirmed on October 9 that her company’s access pathway had been exploited.Pays held authorised access to the national CPR infrastructure to deliver commercial verification services, such as validating business customer records. Following the disclosures, Pays took its corporate website offline and the homepage reflects the message: “Page is under construction. For contact use the information below” with its office address in Denmark.Danish officials confirmed that data relating to 8.8 million people was accessed during the incident. The national registry holds roughly 11 million files overall, a total that includes records for deceased citizens and individuals who have relocated overseas.Internal documents reviewed by Danish broadcaster TV 2 reveal the intruder had free rein inside the national system for over a week. The attacker first penetrated the CPR database on September 10 and between September 10 and September 20, the intruder executed roughly 14 million automated database queries. The intrusion was not uncovered until October 2, nearly two weeks after the automated scraping activity ceased.The unusual activity was caught almost by accident. Mikkel Leihardt, director at the Danish Ministry of Higher Education and Science, explained during a press conference that the breach came to light only after a department staffer flagged a billing invoice showing an abnormally high volume of query activity charged to Pays.Danish data privacy watchdog Datatilsynet was formally alerted on October 4, followed by a public government announcement on October 5.According to password management firm NordPass, "123456" remains the most common – and dangerous – credential on the internet. The firm noted that the simple sequence has retained the top spot as the world's most widely used password in six out of the past seven years (since the starting of the publication of the list) briefly ceding ground only once to “password”.It also says that “12345” and “123456” emerged as the top password choice in every age group: Generation Z, Millennials, Generation X, Baby boomers and Silent generation.
Article Summary: Danish officials confirmed that data relating to 8.8 million people was accessed during the incident. The national registry holds roughly 11 million files overall, a total that includes records for deceased citizens and individuals who have relocated overseas. The intrusion was not uncovered until October 2, nearly two weeks after the automated scraping activity ceased.

Article Title: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney owned thousands of acres in North Carolina, then gave up about one-third of the land’s value in a conservation sale that helped create a state natural area of more than 6,00
Article Text:
Tim Sweeney of Epic Games, with an aerial view of the North Carolina forest. (Image courtesy: Wikimedia Commons)

Tim Sweeney held the Bobs Creek land until North Carolina could afford it

Bobs Creek State Natural Area protects five miles of headwater streams

Bobs Creek is one piece of Tim Sweeney’s 50,000-acre conservation plan

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney is best known as the man behind Fortnite and the Unreal Engine. In his home state of North Carolina, he is also one of the largest private landowners, and a big piece of that land has passed into public hands. Sweeney sold 2,249 acres in McDowell County to the state well below market price, giving up about one-third of the property’s value.That sale completed the Bobs Creek State Natural Area, a protected stretch of foothills forest covering more than 6,000 acres. Foothills Conservancy of North Carolina and the North Carolina Division of Parks and Recreation closed the deal on March 30, 2022. It was the third and final purchase for the project. The first two phases, covering roughly 3,700 acres, were bought in 2019.The discount was only part of the deal. Sweeney had secured the land earlier and held it for years while the conservancy and state parks officials raised the money to buy it. Andrew Kota, executive director of Foothills Conservancy, thanked him for his effort “to secure the land and patiently own it” until the funding came through. The full purchase took four years across three phases.Dwayne Patterson, director of the state parks division, credited “the foresight and generosity of Mr. Sweeney” for making it possible.The final phase was paid for with a $1.2 million grant from the North Carolina Land and Water Fund and $1,518,399 from the federal Land and Water Conservation Fund. Grants from conservationists Fred and Alice Stanback and the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation covered the rest. The state legislature authorised Bobs Creek as a natural area in 2017, and Governor Roy Cooper signed the bill.The state manages the site for passive, low-impact recreation. Plans for the land include hiking trails, mountain biking, wildlife watching and scenic viewpoints.Water is a big reason the land was worth saving. The property guards five miles of source streams that feed Muddy Creek, the Catawba River and the Second Broad River, with wide forest buffers along their banks. The Muddy Creek watershed sits on the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality’s priority list for water quality improvement. The land also holds rare plants and a mix of natural habitats recorded by the state’s Natural Heritage Program.Sweeney has been buying land in North Carolina since 2008 and has acquired more than 50,000 acres across 15 counties, much of it through a holding company called 130 of Chatham LLC. He favours connected tracts over scattered plots, so wildlife can move across large, unbroken stretches of forest.Bobs Creek fills a gap in one such corridor. The chain runs from South Mountains State Park, which spans more than 20,000 acres, through the roughly 7,000-acre Box Creek Wilderness and Bobs Creek, to the Pisgah National Forest in the west. Sweeney placed Box Creek under a permanent easement with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. In 2021, he gave 7,500 acres in the Roan Highlands to the Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy, the largest private land donation in North Carolina’s history.The timing of his purchases has tracked the economy. “Most of my big conservation land purchasing breakthroughs came when the economy was in poor shape and land was prudently priced,” Sweeney said last year. With land prices rising since 2021, he said his focus has moved to putting the large blocks he already owns into permanent conservation.Bobs Creek shows that plan at work. Land that sat in a billionaire’s private portfolio for years is now set aside for North Carolina’s public, for good.
Article Summary: Tim Sweeney sold 2,249 acres in McDowell County to the state well below market price, giving up about one-third of the property’s value. That sale completed the Bobs Creek State Natural Area, a protected stretch of foothills forest covering more than 6,000 acres. Sweeney had secured the land earlier and held it for years while the conservancy and state parks officials raised the money.

Article Title: Google Pay upgrades Flex credit card rewards ahead of festive season; Google One members to get more cashback
Article Text:
Higher rewards on UPI and everyday spending

Additional savings for Google One subscribers

Referral and welcome rewards increased

New Pixel, Fitbit and Google One AI benefits

Google has announced an overhaul of the Google Pay rewards programme for its Flex co-branded credit card, introduced in partnership with Axis Bank and SBI Card, as it looks to attract more users ahead of the festive shopping season. The revised benefits will come into effect from October 16, 2026. Under the updated programme, Google One subscribers will receive significantly higher rewards on everyday spending, while all Flex cardholders will gain access to expanded Google ecosystem benefits, including discounts on Google One AI plans and select Pixel and Fitbit devices.The biggest change is aimed at cardholders who use Flex for regular payments through UPI and other transactions. Google One members holding a Flex credit card will now earn 3.2% back in Stars, with one Star equivalent to ₹1, on all spends during a reward cycle once their total spending exceeds Rs 15,000. Non-Google One members will receive 1.6% back in Stars on all eligible spending after crossing the same ₹15,000 threshold.Google is also introducing category-specific bonuses for Google One members.Eligible users will receive an additional 5% reward on up to Rs 5,000 spent across leading food and grocery applications during each reward cycle.They will also earn an extra 15% reward on up to Rs 3,000 spent on utilities, OTT subscriptions, mobile recharges and related services.The company said these changes are intended to increase value on recurring household and digital-service expenses.Google Pay is also expanding incentives for both new and existing Flex users.The company said it will soon offer Rs 1,000 in rewards for every friend or family member referred to the Flex programme, with no cap on the number of successful referrals.For new applicants, welcome rewards have also been enhanced. Customers applying for a new Flex card can receive welcome benefits worth up to Rs 2,500 within the first 60 days of obtaining the card, depending on the selected card variant.All Flex cardholders will gain access to additional Google ecosystem offers.Starting November 15, 2026, users will be eligible for discounts of up to Rs 3,900 on Google One AI Plus plans, equivalent to a 50% reduction in pricing.Cardholders can also receive discounts of up to Rs 10,000 on the latest Google Pixel smartphones and Fitbit devices purchased from select offline retail stores. Google noted that this offer is currently available only on the Axis Bank variant of the Flex card.
Article Summary: Google Pay overhauls rewards programme for its Flex co-branded credit card. Google One subscribers will receive significantly higher rewards on everyday spending. All Flex cardholders will gain access to expanded Google ecosystem benefits. These include discounts on Google One AI plans and select Pixel and Fitbit devices.

Article Title: Texas rejected a settlement that would have cut a proposed data center from 2,523 acres to 1,375; commissioners also denied the developer’s permit appeal as a court fight now looms
Article Text:
AI image for representation purpose

Why commissioners rejected the settlement

Developer says court action is likely

Why are residents opposing the project

Texas' Hood County commissioners have rejected a settlement that would have reduced a proposed data center project from about 2,523 acres to 1,375 acres. They also unanimously denied the developer's appeal against an earlier decision to reject permits for the project, bringing a possible court fight closer. The decisions came on Tuesday, October 13, after hours of public testimony and debate over the Comanche Circle data center project. Developer Sailfish Investors had reportedly offered to reduce the project's size and make commitments on water-efficient cooling, building setbacks, light pollution and road repairs in an effort to reach an agreement with the county.However, commissioners voted 3-1 against the settlement, with Kevin Andrews the only member voting against its rejection. Commissioner Nanette Samuelson was absent. The commissioners later voted unanimously to deny the developer's permit appeal.The proposed Comanche Circle campus, led by Sailfish managing partner Ryan Hughes, is planned near the Hood and Somervell county line, close to Dinosaur Valley State Park. Residents raised concerns about the project's possible effects on water supplies, wildlife, nearby properties and local roads.Questions were also raised about drainage, power generation and the project's water source. Opponents argued that the developer had not provided enough information and proper plans.Kevin Andrews said the county should continue discussions with the developer rather than reject the settlement.“We have been offered concessions that we can’t regulate, and I think it would be a good idea for us to continue to negotiate to try to get to terms that work for the county,” Andrews said.The proposed settlement included closed-loop cooling, which is designed to reuse cooling water, along with light pollution controls and other commitments. Hughes also said he would not seek tax incentives if the agreement was approved. However, commissioners rejected the deal and then voted against the appeal of the earlier permit decision.In an October 1 email to county officials, Ryan Hughes warned that rejecting the settlement could lead to a lawsuit and potentially leave the project subject to fewer restrictions. Before the vote, he told commissioners, “It looks like we’re unfortunately going to court.”After the decisions, Hughes said he was disappointed but not surprised. In a statement sent to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, he said he had agreed to reduce the project's size and include water-efficient cooling and light pollution controls.“When Governor Abbott set his commonsense data center standards, I agreed with them wholeheartedly and committed Comanche Circle to them,” Hughes wrote.He added: “I hoped today’s settlement would end this dispute for good. Instead, neighbors lose those protections and taxpayers pay for a court fight the County could have avoided,” he said.Hughes also apologised during the meeting for using profanity in text messages discussed by speakers at the hearing.“That’s how I talk to my friends. That’s how I talk to colleagues. And you know, it’s something that my wife says I really hope to work on. So I definitely apologize for the language and apologize for any insinuations,” he said.Residents and local groups, including Protect the Paluxy Valley, have opposed the proposed campus over concerns about its impact on water resources and the surrounding environment. Commissioner Dave Eagle said Hood County has a special designation under state law, known as Subchapter 231K, which covers the watershed that drains into Lake Granbury and the Brazos River.Eagle said the law gives the county powers intended to protect public health and safety and prevent pollution of rivers and lakes. Texas counties are still working out how to regulate large data centre projects while balancing the interests of developers, property owners and local communities.With the settlement rejected and the permit appeal denied, Sailfish Investors faces another setback in its effort to move forward with Comanche Circle. The company had argued that the settlement would allow the project to proceed with additional restrictions, but commissioners chose not to approve the agreement.
Article Summary: Texas' Hood County commissioners rejected a settlement that would have reduced a proposed data center project from about 2,523 acres to 1,375 acres. They also unanimously denied the developer's appeal against an earlier decision to reject permits for the project. Developer Sailfish Investors had reportedly offered to reduce the project's size and make commitments on water-efficient cooling, building setbacks and light pollution.
