Article Title: OpenAI fires employees after spying device found in office; says: FBI’s investigation is ...
Article Text:
OpenAI: 'FBI's investigation is ongoing'

FBI alleges device targeted confidential AI discussions

Employee arrested, faces prison term

No evidence of leaks so far

OpenAI has terminated an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices, with the company saying it referred the matter to the FBI and is continuing to cooperate with an ongoing investigation. According to a report by Fortune, the federal authorities have arrested 35-year-old Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, an OpenAI engineering lead, on allegations that he secretly installed the device in a conference room used for highly confidential company discussions.The incident came to light on September 30 when OpenAI's technical surveillance countermeasures team found a concealed audio-recording device plugged into a USB port behind a television in a conference room, according to the FBI. The device had allegedly been hidden with a piece of toilet paper and was designed to evade detection, featuring advanced encryption, audio-monitoring capabilities and a mechanism for transferring data.In a statement posted on X, OpenAI said it had used its AI models to analyse the device and trace it back to a specific employee who allegedly planted it days earlier."We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices," the company said."We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier."The company added: "We referred the matter to the FBI, and we're grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work."OpenAI also stressed that it has found no evidence that sensitive AI assets or customer information were accessed. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the company said, confirming that the employee had been terminated.According to federal investigators, the conference room regularly hosted discussions involving OpenAI's proprietary research, product plans, business-development opportunities and strategic decisions. The FBI alleged that the device was placed to secretly capture conversations related to the company's advanced AI technologies.FBI Director Kash Patel described the case as a national-security matter. "According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology," Patel said.He added that protecting American artificial intelligence innovation remains a key counterintelligence priority for the bureau.Federal authorities arrested Alfozan on October 9. Prosecutors have charged him with using or attempting to use an electronic device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he could face up to five years in prison.Authorities allege that OpenAI worked with the FBI between the discovery of the device and the arrest, restricting the employee's access to company systems while investigators gathered evidence. CCTV footage and other evidence reportedly linked him to the device, according to the complaint cited by Fortune.It is unclear what Alfozan planned to do with the recordings. Neither OpenAI nor the FBI has found evidence that anything leaked.“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a post on X. The company added that it takes protecting its technology, data and people seriously “as a matter of national importance.” The FBI’s investigation is ongoing.OpenAI said it used its own models to understand the device and to identify which employee planted it. It called the case an example of how AI can help address sophisticated security threats.
Article Summary: OpenAI terminated an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices. The company said it referred the matter to the FBI and is continuing to cooperate with an ongoing investigation. Abdulrahman Alfozan, an OpenAI engineering lead, was arrested on allegations that he secretly installed the device in a conference room used for confidential company discussions.

Article Title: US Department of Homeland Security removes 540-day grace period for immigrants after their work authorisation expires; here's what the new rules say
Article Text:
What the rule says

Why the 540-day extension existed

Who will be affected

USCIS faces large backlog

Legal challenge ahead

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has moved to permanently end a policy that allowed many immigrants to continue working for up to 540 days after their employment authorisation expired while renewal applications were pending, according to a Bloomberg Law report. The final rule, released this week, makes permanent an interim measure introduced last year that scrapped the Biden-era 540-day automatic extension period for certain categories of foreign workers. The change is set to take effect when it is published in the Federal Register on October 14.* The automatic extension of work permits during renewal is eliminated, so workers lose authorization when their permit expires, even if a renewal is pending.* The final rule takes effect when it is published in the Federal Register on Oct. 14.* Foreign workers cannot apply to renew their documents until 180 days before expiration.The extension window was designed to ensure immigrant workers were not pushed out of jobs because of processing delays at US Citizenship and Immigration Services. The agency has since added a number of hurdles under the Trump administration for immigrants to keep or renew their employment authorization.The policy affects several groups of immigrants who rely on Employment Authorisation Documents (EADs), including asylum seekers and spouses of H-1B visa holders on H-4 visas. DHS said the move would enable more frequent vetting of applicants seeking employment authorisation. The agency argues that shorter extension periods allow authorities to conduct updated eligibility and security reviews more regularly.Despite the change, USCIS continues to deal with significant renewal delays.According to agency data cited by Bloomberg Law, more than 432,000 work permit renewal applications had been pending for six months or longer as of June 30. Of those, more than 91,000 applications had been awaiting a decision for over 18 months.At the same time, foreign workers are generally not permitted to file renewal applications more than 180 days before their current work permits expire, limiting their ability to offset lengthy processing times.The policy has already faced legal scrutiny. A group of H-4 visa holders filed a lawsuit against DHS in January, arguing that the agency's decision to end the longer automatic extension period violated the Administrative Procedure Act. Last month, a federal judge in California issued a limited injunction blocking enforcement of the interim rule against the plaintiffs involved in the case. The court found that DHS had not adequately followed procedural requirements and failed to address the reliance interests of affected individuals.
Article Summary: US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has moved to permanently end a policy that allowed many immigrants to continue working for up to 540 days after their employment authorisation expired. The final rule, released this week, makes permanent an interim measure introduced last year that scrapped the 540-day automatic extension period. The change is set to take effect when it is published in the Federal Register on October 14.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says AI has made coding faster, but it has not yet …
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu

Sridhar Vembu: AI is increasing costs for software companies

The US stock market is in a monster bubble and it is a mistake to think of stock prices as indicative of future prosperity - the GFC of 2008-9, dotcom bust of 2001-2 as wall as the 1980s Japan bubble all demonstrate that point,” Vembu added.

Sridhar Vembu: 10x productivity leap in software is coming

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu said that AI is making software development faster, but it has not yet made the process 10 or 100 times more productive. Sharing a post on X (formerly Twitter), Vembu said that such a leap could happen in the future, putting pressure on software jobs. “As of today, AI led productivity gain in software development estimates are (at best) 25% to 50% as measured on an end to end product basis (prototyping is much much faster now but finished product requires a lot more human work),” he said in the post adding “A 10x or 100x productivity leap could happen (I believe it will happen, see below) but it has not happened _yet_”.In the post, Sridhar Vembu also pointed to three major expenses that companies are incurring because of AI. These include:Vembu says that the 10x productivity leap in software is coming “because of what is happening in the mathematics world. The crucial link is auto-formalization, or formal verification of code. Mathematics theorems are formalized in Lean and proofs are verified by the Lean verifier - Lean is a programming language”.“LLMs do not verify the proof, they generate it to be verified by the Lean verifier and once you have the advanced reasoning capable LLM and Lean verifier in a feedback loop and give plenty of compute, magic happens,” he said.He also shared an analogy explaining how formal automated verification mechanism is coming to LLM generated software. “The analogy is handloom weaving vs powerful machine looms of code,” he wrote.Concluding the post, Vembu wrote “So it is the combination of current data center/AI costs, geopolitical uncertainty and the potential of a 10x or bigger leap in software productivity driven by advances in automatic program verification. These are all challenges to software jobs, and that is why we have called for reinvention internally”.
Article Summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu said that AI is making software development faster, but it has not yet made the process 10 or 100 times more productive. He said that such a leap could happen in the future, putting pressure on software jobs. He pointed to three major expenses that companies are incurring because of AI.

Article Title: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar has an 'AI theory' for more researchers taking up smoking; says: These folks in Silicon Valley have filled hole in their hearts with God of ...
Article Text:
Shyam Sankar blames effective altruism for AI doomsday fears

Palantir CTO wants existing laws to govern how AI is used

Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar has an unusual explanation for why some AI researchers are picking up cigarettes. According to him, lighting up is their way of telling peers just how firmly they believe artificial intelligence will one day cure cancer. Sankar made the remark in a US television interview on Sunday, while arguing that fear-driven narratives are muddying the AI safety debate. He did not name any researchers or offer evidence. "So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI," he said. The smoker's message, in his words, is: "I'm showing you my chips are all in."The claim was part of a bigger argument. Citing philosopher Blaise Pascal's idea that every human has a "god-shaped hole" in their heart, Sankar said many people building this technology in Silicon Valley "have filled that hole with the machine God of AGI." He called the mood around it a "mass psychosis."Sankar traced much of the AI anxiety to effective altruism, which he described as a "doomsday cult." Its most famous follower, he noted, is jailed crypto founder Sam Bankman-Fried. By his count, America has roughly 2,000 AI researchers, and most of them share that worldview.So when a researcher like Jacob Coxon warns that AI has a 10% chance of ending humanity, Sankar wants people to treat it as a theological critique rather than a scientific one.He also pointed out that doomsayers once called GPT-2 too dangerous to release and predicted mass unemployment that has not arrived.Sankar insisted he is not against guardrails. He wants rules aimed at how AI is applied, with the FDA watching over medicine and the Department of Transportation over transport. His analogy: a defective car is the carmaker's problem, but driving it into a neighbour's house is yours.He also noted that some frontier models are now being held back from release, which he said would have been unthinkable a year ago.The smoking claim, for now, rests on his word. A small circle of tech founders and investors has embraced cigarettes, and Avi Schiffmann, founder of AI wearable startup Friend, has said AI should have cured lung cancer by the time smokers get it. Medicine is yet to share that confidence. Smoking remains a leading cause of preventable death worldwide.
Article Summary: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar blames effective altruism for AI doomsday fears. He wants existing laws to govern how AI is used in medicine and transport. He did not name any researchers or offer evidence for his claim.

Article Title: How hackers taking control of hundreds of refrigerators in supermarkets across France may have 'proved' Europe's fears of China deactivating hundreds of its buses right on the roads 'true'
Article Text:
The French refrigerator attack

Echoing Europe’s nightmare over Chinese connected buses

A cyberattack that hijacked commercial refrigeration units across hundreds of French supermarkets has offered a real-world demonstration of the dangers lurking in connected infrastructure. For European officials, the incident does more than spotlight digital vulnerabilities in the food supply – it provides a warning and fuel to growing anxieties across the region that internet-linked transit systems, including hundreds of public buses built by Chinese manufacturers, could be remotely immobilised right on the roads during a crisis.The Paris prosecutor’s office launched an investigation this week following an overnight cyberattack targeting cooling systems across multiple French grocery chains. Attackers breached central management panels, overriding controls to force refrigeration and freezer units into non-stop defrost cycles at 50°C (122°F). This resulted in fires, melted equipment and dumpsters full of spoiled food, with French retail group Les Mousquetaires (operator of Intermarché and Netto) reporting losses reaching millions of euros.France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) confirmed the attack targeted Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series controllers.Danfoss acknowledged the breach, stating the affected units ran “outdated firmware” and noting that it “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions.”The supermarket breach underscores a core vulnerability: once a piece of infrastructure is connected online for diagnostics, anyone with system-level access – whether a malicious hacker or the manufacturer itself – can override its physical operations.That exact mechanism was at the heart of the panic in Scandinavia, where transport operators in Denmark and Norway, last year, started probing Chinese-built electric buses over fears they could be remotely weaponized or shut down.Scrutiny centered on Yutong, the Zhengzhou-based company that ranks as the world’s largest bus maker by sales volume. Danish transport operator Movia, which runs 262 Yutong buses across Copenhagen and eastern Denmark, warned that over-the-air (OTA) functionality creates severe exposure.“Because these buses can receive updates and diagnostic tests 'over the air,' they can be stopped remotely, either by the manufacturer or by a hacker,” Movia COO Jeppe Gaard told NBC News.Norwegian transit agency Ruter, which oversees half of Norway’s public transport, conducted controlled tests “inside a mountain” comparing Yutong vehicles against Dutch-made VDL models. While Dutch buses lacked automated OTA functions, Yutong maintained “direct digital access to each individual bus,” leading Ruter to conclude that the fleet could, in theory, be rendered completely inoperable by the manufacturer.In response, Yutong stressed that it “strictly complies with the applicable laws, regulations, and industry standards,” noting that its European Union operational data is encrypted and housed in an Amazon Web Services facility in Frankfurt, Germany.
Article Summary: Attackers hijacked commercial refrigeration units across hundreds of French supermarkets. French retail group Les Mousquetaires ( operator of Intermarché and Netto) reported losses reaching millions of euros. The supermarket breach underscores a core vulnerability: once a piece of infrastructure is connected online for diagnostics, anyone with system-level access can override its physical operations.

Article Title: Michael Dell joins debate on 'safeguards and controls' for AI models; sends 'strong message' to government, OpenAI and Anthropic
Article Text:
AI is not wiping humanity

Sees no AI bubble

Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell warned that artificial intelligence requires strict safeguards and controls, weighing in on an escalating national debate over the existential risks posed by rapidly advancing AI systems. Speaking on CNBC, Dell framed the emergence of artificial intelligence through the lens of foundational human technologies. “I think we’ve always had technology that can do great things and maybe do some not-so-great things,” Dell said. “You know, fire can heat your home. It can also burn down your whole village. So that’s not good. So we have to have safeguards and controls.”Dell emphasized that both the public and private sectors bear responsibility for managing these risks. While calling on AI developers to establish "bounded permissions" within their tools, he acknowledged that government intervention is necessary. However, Dell declined to outline specific legislative or policy measures, noting that he is not a policymaker.Dell also doesn't believe that AI is coming to kill humans. He disagrees with the view that AI will destroy humanity by 2030; says, "It will be fine."His remarks arrive amid growing alarm from researchers and industry veterans over catastrophic risks tied to recursive, self-improving models.The current wave of scrutiny gained momentum following an early September warning from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who resigned after publicly arguing that frontier laboratories are gambling with human lives in an unchecked pursuit of superintelligence.Coxon’s departure galvanized prominent tech executives, with leaders such as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei voicing support for regulatory intervention and a coordinated pause in frontier model deployment.Michael Dell also dismissed concerns about an AI bubble, pointing to a shortage of computing capacity and rising rental prices for Nvidia's H100 chips as signs of sustained demand. "I don't think there's enough supply for it to be a bubble," Dell said. He further pointed to the strong demand for compute. He added that customers are seeing significant returns from using computing resources to generate intelligence.Despite those calls, the Trump administration has resisted mandatory pauses and statutory guardrails. At a White House luncheon late last month, President Donald Trump gathered leading tech executives to sign a voluntary, "morally binding" pact pledging to self-regulate system safety alongside independent evaluators.That voluntary agreement has largely stalled formal federal regulation, even as public anxiety mounts over AI safety and the sweeping footprint of data center expansion. With the midterm elections just weeks away, the debate surrounding artificial intelligence oversight has emerged as a pivotal battleground that could determine which party controls Congress for the remainder of Trump’s term.
Article Summary: Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell warned that artificial intelligence requires strict safeguards and controls. Dell emphasized that both the public and private sectors bear responsibility for managing these risks. Dell also dismissed concerns about an AI bubble, pointing to a shortage of computing capacity and rising rental prices for Nvidia's H100 chips.

Article Title: Scientists discover ‘hidden materials’ that may lead to better batteries and solar fuels
Article Text:
Representational image

Why this discovery is important

Uncovering 'new form' of Bismuth Vanadate

Promising breakthrough for next-generation batteries

An international research team has uncovered a class of previously unknown “hidden materials” by tracking the elusive, split-second changes that occur as molecules decompose under heat. The findings, published in Nature Communications, may unlock new pathways to develop more efficient solar fuel systems and higher-capacity batteries.Typically, when materials scientists create solid compounds through thermal processing, attention is paid almost entirely to the final outcome – which is essentially moving straight from starting material “A” to end product “B.” However, by freezing and analysing the fleeting intermediate phases that arise during the heating cycle, researchers discovered entirely new structures that are difficult or impossible to manufacture using standard synthesis methods.“When materials are made by heating, scientists usually focus on the final product, the 'B' that results from 'A.' But this study shows that there are many fascinating stages in between 'A' and 'B,' and these hidden steps could be just as important,” said Dr. Sebastian Pike from the Department of Chemistry at the University of Warwick.“We didn't know exactly what we would find going in, but we were confident there would be something interesting and unknown in the intermediate phases.We were thrilled to discover that some of these could have practical uses, even from the very first experiments,” Pike added.The team began their experiments using customised “single-source precursors” – single molecules engineered to contain every fundamental element required to yield a targeted solid material. As temperatures steadily rose, the scientists monitored how the molecular bonds broke apart and reassembled. This tracking exposed several uncharted material phases, most notably a newly discovered, kinetically stabilized form of bismuth vanadate.Standard bismuth vanadate has been prized in renewable energy engineering due to its optimal “band gap” – the exact energy threshold needed to absorb sunlight and catalyze chemical reactions. This characteristic allows it to harvest solar energy efficiently while providing the required chemical punch to split water molecules into clean hydrogen fuel.The newly identified ‘form’ features a distinct atomic architecture that sets it apart from all previously cataloged variations of the compound. Crucially, it possesses a significantly wider band gap, fundamentally changing how the material absorbs and reacts to light. Researchers note that this shift introduces fresh avenues to fine-tune materials across catalysis, advanced electronics, and solar fuel generation.The utility of these intermediate materials extends beyond solar energy. During the testing process, the scientists isolated another transient phase exhibiting high-capacity lithium storage, suggesting immediate promise for next-generation battery architectures.“What's exciting is that these 'in-between' materials aren't just stepping stones — they can have useful properties in their own right,” explained Dr. Dominik Kubicki from the School of Chemistry at the University of Birmingham. “By understanding and controlling how they form, we can start to design better materials for batteries, catalysis, and solar energy.”
Article Summary: University of Warwick researchers have discovered a class of previously unknown 'hidden materials' by tracking the elusive, split-second changes that occur as molecules decompose under heat. The findings may unlock new pathways to develop more efficient solar fuel systems and higher-capacity batteries.

Article Title: Bumble is off the market, agrees to go private in $1.3 billion deal
Article Text:
A $1.3 billion match for Bumble (Picture: Reuters)

Why Bumble decided it was time to sell

Bumble's new co-CEOs are counting on AI to bring daters back

Bumble is going private. The dating app has agreed to be acquired by Ithaca Holdings in a $1.3 billion deal, and Ithaca co-founders Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman will become Bumble's co-CEOs once it closes. Founder Whitney Wolfe Herd, who started the app 12 years ago, will stay actively involved, though her exact role hasn't been spelled out.Ithaca is paying $6.05 per share, a 122.4% premium to Bumble's closing price on June 24, the day before reports emerged that the company was exploring a sale. Investors liked what they saw. The stock jumped 50% on Monday as news of the deal spread and rose another 56% to $5.95 in early trading on Tuesday. Even so, Bumble was worth only about $582 million at Monday's close, far below the roughly $14 billion valuation it fetched on its Nasdaq debut in 2021.An independent committee of Bumble's board recommended the deal after a review of strategic options, and Wolfe Herd stayed out of the discussions and the vote. Blackstone, which owns about 14% of Bumble, has signed off alongside her, giving the deal the shareholder approval it needs.The reasons for selling are in the numbers. Bumble's second-quarter revenue fell 15.2% year-on-year to $211 million, while paying users dropped 16.4% to around 3.2 million. Revenue has been sliding for close to two years, and the company has turned an annual pre-tax profit only once since going public. Last year, it cut nearly a third of its workforce.Gupta held C-suite roles at Instacart before becoming a partner at Sequoia, and Hegeman was previously Meta's chief revenue officer. They will be the first men to lead the women-first app since it listed. The pair described the acquisition as "a bet on the future of humanity", with Ithaca focused on building businesses for a world reshaped by AI.Bumble was already moving that way. Since Wolfe Herd returned as CEO in March 2025, it has added AI help for profiles and messages, started testing an AI matchmaking assistant and introduced Plans in July, which nudges users towards real-world meetups. In August, it scrapped the rule that only women could message first, the very feature that built the brand. Wolfe Herd has also teased a new way to interact that could eventually replace swiping.Rival Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, has also slumped from its 2021 highs, but Hinge keeps pulling in people after serious relationships. Away from public markets, Bumble now gets time to prove it can win those daters back.
Article Summary: Ithaca is paying $6.05 per share, a 122.4% premium to Bumble's closing price on June 24. Founder Whitney Wolfe Herd, who started the app 12 years ago, will stay actively involved, though her exact role hasn't been spelled out. The company has turned an annual pre-tax profit only once since going public.

Article Title: Godfather of AI Yann LeCun opposes Dario Amodei’s call of slowing down AI development, says ‘Anthropic is trying to scare governments by saying…’
Article Text:
Yann LeCun opposes Anthropic: ‘No different from anti-enlightenment’

Yann LeCun, Turing Award winner and widely recognised as one of the three “godfathers of AI,” has pushed back against calls to slow down artificial intelligence (AI) development, accusing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei of using alarmist messaging to lobby regulators and restrict public access to the technology. Speaking during an interview on the morning of October 12 at the Westin Chosun Seoul in Jung-gu, the co-founder and chairman of AMI Labs addressed the intensifying divide across Silicon Valley over safety regulations and model releases.“It’s natural for companies to release products with safety measures to prevent harm to people,” said LeCun, who won the 2018 Turing Award alongside Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton for pioneering the foundations of computer vision and image recognition, was in South Korea for the Industrial AI Global Cooperation Meeting ahead of the IIAC 2026 conference in Tokyo.“However, large language models (LLMs) are difficult to fine-tune, so they can potentially harm humans in certain cases. Sam Altman says, ‘We’ll release them cautiously,’ while Dario Amodei argues, ‘They’re too dangerous to manage and shouldn’t be given to the public.’ I oppose Dario’s view,” he added, as per a report in South Korean publication Chosun.LeCun compared attempts to gatekeep underlying model weights to historical efforts to suppress information.“Restricting access is no different from anti-enlightenment – like the Ottoman Empire banning printing in the 15th century to prevent information from reaching people. Ultimately, foundational AI models should be open-source. Only then can human culture, knowledge, and information spread.”When asked whether modern systems can be controlled, LeCun dismissed the notion that today’s large language models pose an existential threat to society. Instead, he framed alarmist narratives as political leverage.“I don’t think current AI is dangerous. The argument for slowing down AI development is a form of marketing or lobbying. Anthropic is portraying AI as extremely dangerous to scare governments. But LLMs aren’t at that level yet.”While talking about the Hugging Face incident, where an OpenAI model attempted to break out of its environment, LeCun argued that such occurrences stem from poor supervision rather than machine malice.“The Hugging Face incident happened due to intentional or incompetent design flaws. Human supervisors failed to properly design the experimental environment, causing AI agents to deviate. Since these agents aren’t inherently malicious, no harm occurred.”Later during the meeting, LeCun reiterated that governing artificial intelligence is fundamentally a technical challenge rather than a crisis of control.
Article Summary: Yann LeCun says Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is using alarmist messaging to lobby regulators and restrict public access to the technology. He was in South Korea for the Industrial AI Global Cooperation Meeting ahead of the IIAC 2026 conference in Tokyo.

Article Title: Workday announces new AI agents, Sana experience and C1.ai acquisition at Rising 2026 event
Article Text:
Workday to acquire C1.ai for agentic identity management

Sana becomes the new Workday Home with AI agents

Workday launches Autopilot Agents across HR, finance and IT

Trusted Agent Platform gets headless access

New tools target recruitment and business decisions

Workday expands Anthropic partnership and brings Sana to other platforms

Workday has announced a series of AI updates at its Rising 2026 event. The enterprise software company has signed a definitive agreement to acquire C1.ai, an agentic identity management platform, and introduced new AI agents designed to handle tasks across human resources (HR), finance, and IT. The announcements also include a redesigned Workday Home powered by Sana, a platform that lets customers build and manage their own AI agents, along with new tools for workforce planning and financial decisions.Workday is also expanding its partnerships with Anthropic and other technology companies to bring its AI capabilities into the tools employees already use. The updates reflect the company's push to move AI beyond answering questions towards completing business tasks.Workday has signed a definitive agreement to acquire C1.ai, a platform focused on identity management for people and AI agents. The acquisition is intended to help Workday manage access to applications, data and systems for employees and AI agents throughout their lifecycle.With the acquisition, Workday aims to establish an identity governance layer covering people, money and agents. The system is designed to ensure employees and AI agents receive the right access permissions when they join an organisation, change roles, or leave.The move comes as businesses increasingly deploy AI agents to perform tasks across enterprise systems, creating a need to manage their access and permissions alongside those of human employees.Workday has introduced Sana as the new Workday Home, describing it as an agentic experience designed to complete tasks rather than simply answer questions.Employees can make requests in natural language, and Sana coordinates the relevant Workday AI agents to carry out the requested actions. The company said Sana Concierge can handle HR and IT requests, including employee onboarding and password resets, before they become support tickets.Workday is positioning Sana as an interface that lets employees access business services and get work done without navigating multiple systems or manually completing every step.Workday has also launched Autopilot Agents that operate in the background across HR, finance and IT. The agents are designed to handle tasks involving hiring, payroll, accounting and compliance.According to the company, the agents can identify work that needs attention and recommend actions or take them within customer-defined policies and approval limits. Sana coordinates their activities, while existing business rules determine what they can do independently.The objective is to reduce the time employees spend on routine operational tasks, allowing teams to focus on decisions that require human judgement.Workday's Trusted Agent Platform now supports headless access to HR and finance capabilities, allowing customers to build, run and govern their own AI agents.The company said Agent-Ready Tools, Agent Harness, Developer Agent, Custom Agents and Data Cloud are generally available. These capabilities support different AI models and development frameworks.Workday, customer-built and partner-developed agents operate under the same permissions, approval processes and audit trails, according to the company. The approach is intended to give organisations flexibility in developing AI agents while retaining governance over how they access and use business data.Workday has announced additional features for recruitment, workforce planning and financial analysis. The new Candidate Profile feature allows job seekers to save their information once and reuse it when applying to companies that use Workday for recruitment. The company aims to reduce friction in the application process and address an estimated application-abandonment rate of around 60%.Workday Decision Intelligence is now available across the company's portfolio. The AI-powered HR and finance analyst helps teams model scenarios using live, governed Workday data. Businesses can compare hiring strategies, identify skills gaps and analyse financial variances before routing recommendations through existing approval processes.Workday has also introduced Work Intelligence, which helps organisations break jobs into individual tasks and map them to the skills required to perform them. Using Workday Skills Cloud's database of more than 75,000 skills, the tool helps leaders determine which tasks AI can automate, which it can support, and which should remain with people.Workday and Anthropic have announced a partnership connecting Claude's reasoning capabilities with Sana AI agents and Workday's business data and context. Depending on the task, users can access the experience through Sana or Claude.Workday is also expanding Sana's availability beyond its own platform. The agentic experience and orchestration engine will work within tools employees already use, including Claude, Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise, Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams and Slack. The integrations let employees access Workday capabilities through existing workplace tools rather than switching between applications.
Article Summary: Workday has signed a definitive agreement to acquire C1.ai, an agentic identity management platform. The company has introduced new AI agents designed to handle tasks across human resources (HR), finance, and IT. Workday is also expanding its partnerships with Anthropic and other technology companies to bring its AI capabilities into the tools employees already use.

Article Title: Microsoft has bought more than 600 acres in an Iowa town of about 1,300 people for a proposed data center; more than 200 residents packed a school meeting as the company outlined roads, utilities and
Article Text:
Representative Image

How Microsoft’s purchase of more than 600 acres in Woodward sets the stage for a data center

What Microsoft told more than 200 residents about roads, utilities and electricity

Why Woodward residents questioned the lack of community involvement

“Is this something that we get a vote on? I mean, something this big, the community should get to vote on instead of doing back-end deals,”

“I can safely say I have not seen a single one of you at a budget meeting when we try to balance a budget for this community,”

“We have to find revenue sources for our community.”

Why the residents-only meeting drew criticism over public access

“It runs counter to the openness that the public meetings all guarantee,”

“From my vantage point, it erodes the trust and confidence, and the respect for Woodward city government.”

A proposed Microsoft data center in a small town in Iowa may have triggered concerns over the area’s future. The tech giant has reportedly purchased more than 600 acres of industrially zoned land in Iowa’s Woodward community last week. This sets the stage for a potential development that could reshape the town's tax base and infrastructure.According to a KCCI report, more than 200 residents gathered at Woodward-Granger High School this week to hear Microsoft representatives and Mayor Todd Folkerts explain preliminary plans, including roads, water and sewer upgrades, and electricity arrangements. The meeting also exposed residents’ concerns about limited community involvement, environmental effects of the planned data centre, and whether a project of this scale should require a public vote.Microsoft completed the purchase of approximately 600 acres in the Woodward Eco Business Park last week, the report noted. The property was acquired from an independent seller rather than the city and is already zoned for industrial use, which permits data center development.The business park received certified-site status in 2018, making it a potential location for industrial projects.However, Microsoft has not yet designed the proposed data center, and company representatives said the design process could take roughly two years before construction could begin.The project would be located on the southern side of Woodward, a community of approximately 1,300 people. Its scale has raised questions about how the development would affect the town’s infrastructure, environment and quality of life.Microsoft representatives met with Folkerts for a 90-minute session at Woodward-Granger High School on Monday. The session brought residents and company officials together to discuss the proposal and answer questions about its potential impact.The company said it would pay for the infrastructure required for the project, including road construction and paving, water and sewer upgrades, and electricity infrastructure. Government Affairs Infrastructure Director Cloteal LaBroi said the company’s plans would also include arrangements designed to limit the project's impact on existing municipal services.Microsoft said a closed-loop cooling system would not affect the city's water resources. It also plans to buy electricity directly from a wholesaler, which representatives said would keep the project from affecting the local power grid or raising electricity rates for residents.Company officials said the data center would create dozens of jobs and contribute to the town’s tax base. However, the facility’s final design and construction timeline remain uncertain.Though Microsoft assured infrastructure and economic benefits, some residents seemed frustrated with the land-acquisition process. Some asked whether town residents had a right to speak on an issue that might have a huge impact on their lives.one resident said.Folkerts responded that residents would not vote directly on the proposal. Instead, the city council would vote on negotiations between Microsoft and the city, and the council would have to approve a development agreement before the project could move forward. The council would also need to approve a site plan later.Defending the need to find additional revenue for the town, Folkerts told the gathering:he said to the crowd.The meeting also attracted criticism over restrictions on who could attend. It replaced the city's regular council meeting but was limited to Woodward residents, who had to show proof of residency to enter. Several people were turned away.Randy Evans, president of Iowa’s Freedom of Information Council, was among those denied entry. He questioned whether the restriction was consistent with Iowa's open meeting laws.Evans told KCCI.Tensions also surfaced inside the auditorium, where police escorted out a vocal opponent after an altercation during the meeting. Outside, about half a dozen protesters gathered to oppose data center developments, including projects proposed in Ames and Boone.
Article Summary: Microsoft has reportedly purchased more than 600 acres of industrially zoned land in Iowa’s Woodward community. This sets the stage for a potential development that could reshape the town's tax base and infrastructure. More than 200 residents gathered at Woodward-Granger High School this week to hear Microsoft representatives and Mayor Todd Folkerts explain preliminary plans.

Article Title: Chinese companies 'once again tell' America: You can not keep Nvidia away from us
Article Text:
Representative Image

Chinese companies turn to Nvidia chips amid AI computing shortage

“We believe China’s AI compute expansion has so far been constrained less by demand than by availability of high-end compute,”

“China’s domestic makers of workstation chips and cards have experienced unprecedented growth since 2022.

US firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated US export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly a half a decade ago, and China’s own limits on US imports.”

Nvidia's CUDA software remains a factor for Chinese companies

China's AI spending adds pressure on chip supplies

“There is a consensus across the industry that the current shortage in AI compute will not be resolved until at least 2030,”

Nvidia looks to retain its position in China

“Regulators are talking with tech companies to find out if their demand for Nvidia’s RTX 5500 is necessary,”

“The honest conclusion will be ‘yes’.”

Nvidia still seems to be central to China's artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions. Despite years of US export restrictions aimed at limiting China's access to advanced AI processors, Chinese tech companies have reportedly bought more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation chips this year to address a growing computing-power shortage.According to a report by The Financial Times, Chinese companies are now turning to Nvidia products that comply with US export controls, even as they work to build alternatives that could eventually reduce their reliance on the American chipmaker. The purchases highlight how difficult it has been for Beijing to reduce its dependence on American technology while rapidly expanding its AI infrastructure. Chinese chipmakers, including Huawei, Alibaba, Baidu and Cambricon, are increasing production, but supply has struggled to keep pace with demand from technology companies developing AI models and data centres.The report cited industry insiders, who said Chinese technology companies have purchased more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation processors this year. The chips include the RTX Pro 6000D, RTX Pro 5000 and RTX 5090, which were not designed specifically for advanced AI workloads but can be repurposed for certain computing tasks.The shortage has emerged as China accelerates its efforts to develop domestic alternatives to American AI hardware.Industry insiders estimate that available AI chip supply could reach 3.5 million units this year, including around 1 million manufactured overseas. However, total demand is expected to exceed 5 million units.said Gary Yu, a Morgan Stanley analyst based in Hong Kong.Nvidia said,Beyond hardware availability, Nvidia's CUDA software platform is another reason Chinese tech companies keep seeking its processors. CUDA lets developers use graphics processing units for general computing tasks and has become a standard part of many AI development workflows.Chinese companies are being encouraged to move towards domestic alternatives, including Huawei's CANN software platform. However, transitioning existing systems and workflows to a different software ecosystem presents challenges.DeepSeek is working with Huawei to improve its hardware and software capabilities, while Huawei is also using AI tools to accelerate the migration of programming code from CUDA to CANN.Meanwhile, Chinese companies are investing in domestic processors. Huawei is expected to produce 1.6 million AI chips this year, while Alibaba and Baidu's chip divisions are expected to manufacture a combined 1 million units. Cambricon is projected to produce around 300,000 chips, according to people familiar with the companies' plans.Alibaba recently introduced its Zhenwu V900 processor, while Huawei is developing large computing clusters that connect multiple processors to compensate for performance differences between individual chips.The demand for computing power has increased as Alibaba, ByteDance and Tencent invest in AI models, data centres and agentic AI tools. Their combined capital expenditure this year could more than double to approximately RMB 700 billion, or $104 billion, according to people familiar with the matter.Alibaba chief executive Eddie Wu said during the company's August earnings call.The shortage is also prompting Chinese AI developers to secure computing capacity overseas. Tencent has signed an agreement with Oracle to lease 100,000 GPUs across data centres in Southeast Asia, while ByteDance and Alibaba are pursuing similar arrangements, according to the report.These overseas facilities use Nvidia's advanced processors, including the B300, giving Chinese companies access to computing resources that remain hard to obtain domestically.Nvidia is preparing another workstation processor, the RTX Pro 5500, which is expected to offer higher performance than its existing products available in China. According to two people familiar with the move, Chinese companies have already indicated orders exceeding 2 million units, with shipments potentially beginning towards the end of this year. However, Chinese regulators are examining whether demand for the processor is justified.said one executive at a leading Chinese technology company.The developments underline the challenge facing both Washington and Beijing. US restrictions aim to limit China's access to advanced computing technology, while Beijing works to build a self-sufficient chip industry. Yet rising AI demand and the continued importance of Nvidia's hardware and software show why Chinese tech companies haven't been able to move away from the American chipmaker as quickly as intended.
Article Summary: Chinese companies turn to Nvidia chips amid AI computing shortage. shortage has emerged as China accelerates its efforts to develop domestic alternatives to American AI hardware. Industry insiders estimate that available AI chip supply could reach 3.5 million units this year. However, total demand is expected to exceed 5 million units.

Article Title: How hackers took control of hundreds of refrigerators in supermarkets across France, raising the temperature to 50 degree celsius sparking fires and spoiling food
Article Text:
France supermarket cyberattack: Hackers turn refrigerators into ovens, heating them to 50°C, spoiling food at hundreds of stores

How hackers took control of freezers in France

Cyberattacks are moving well beyond stealing email account passwords, corporate data breaches and compromising smartphones. A wave of cyberattacks have impacted people’s dinner tables in France. Media reports pouring in from the country say that the Paris prosecutor’s office has launched an investigation following an overnight cyberattack that seized remote control of commercial refrigeration and freezer units across hundreds of French supermarkets. By overriding internal heating controls, attackers forced temperatures up to 50°C (122°F), triggering small fires, melting cooling equipment and destroying vast stockpiles of perishable food.French retail giant Les Mousquetaires, which operates the Intermarché and Netto supermarket chains, confirmed that damages will reach several million euros, while Intermarché CEO Thierry Cotillard told broadcaster BFM-TV that the incident triggered losses totaling “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.”“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” Dominique Schelcher, CEO of French grocery chain Coopérative U, wrote in a statement on X.According to BFM-TV, the hackers remotely executed forced, continuous defrost cycles across impacted grocery locations. Rather than maintaining freezing conditions, systems were dialed up to 50°C. According to reporting from Le Monde, attackers also manipulated safety parameters by extending defrost cycles inside freezers and cold rooms from the standard one-hour duration up to eight hours, a deliberate step designed to suppress and delay automated alarm systems.Supermarkets deploy centralised industrial control panels to govern multiple refrigeration lines, often connecting them directly to the internet so external contractors can run diagnostics and maintenance remotely.The French government warned that exposing industrial management dashboards to the public internet violates cybersecurity best practices, stating that remote access should always be strictly cordoned off behind trusted IP addresses.An alert issued by France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) revealed that the attackers targeted two specific refrigeration controller models manufactured by Danish industrial group Danfoss: the AK-SC and AK-SM series.In response, Danfoss acknowledged that it was aware of the disruptions in France, maintaining that the incident was isolated to units operating unpatched code.“The affected units were running outdated firmware,” Danfoss stated, noting that it has “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions.”
Article Summary: Hackers seized remote control of commercial refrigeration and freezer units across hundreds of French supermarkets. By overriding internal heating controls, attackers forced temperatures up to 50°C (122°F) French retail giant Les Mousquetaires, which operates the Intermarché and Netto supermarket chains, confirmed that damages will reach several million euros.
